problem: Earlier object-navigation agents in AI2-THOR (A3C baseline, Scene Priors, SAVN, ORG) condition the policy directly on the target-object embedding or on object-object graphs. When the target is not in view they get little guidance and waste actions spinning and backing up. Their object relations are also either too generic (from Visual Genome) or too tied to specific environments, so they generalize poorly across unseen room layouts.
motivation: Groups of related objects form larger regions, called zones (e.g. sofa+pillow+table, or microwave+sink+stove). Zones are easier to observe than a single small target. Humans look for the typical area first and then the object. So a learned prior over zones and how they are adjacent, adapted online to the current unseen room, should give coarse-to-fine sub-goals that make navigation more efficient.
key_idea: Build a hierarchical scene→zone→object graph from training rooms (zones = K-Means clusters of bag-of-objects views, edges = zone adjacency probability), update it online during each episode, plan a max-probability zone-to-zone path to the target's zone, and feed the next zone on that path as a sub-goal embedding to an A3C LSTM policy.
insight: Guiding with the next sub-goal zone works better than guiding with the target zone: training and testing on the sub-goal zone gives 70.57 vs 69.16 SR and 40.84 vs 39.05 SPL (Table 1). The graph's content matters, not just the extra parameters. Randomizing both nodes and edges drops SR from 70.47 to 67.81 and SAE from 27.85 to 24.13 (Table 7). Defining zones by visual object co-occurrence alone generalizes better than also clustering on location (70.62 vs 68.22 SR), because location restricts zones to the vicinity of objects. The object layer gives the largest single gain (57.35→65.12 SR); the scene and zone layers mostly raise SPL and SAE. Test-time self-supervision (TPN) raises SR but not SPL, so it adds actions. HOZ is complementary to a SLAM-style semantic map: SemExp+HOZ improves over SemExp in Gibson.
method: Room-wise HOZ graph: an agent randomly explores each training room and collects (f, l) pairs, where f is a binary bag-of-objects vector from a fine-tuned Faster R-CNN (22 categories) and l is the pose. K-Means (K=8) on f gives zone nodes; each node's feature is the cluster mean, i.e. object co-occurrence frequency. The edge e(v_k, v_j) is the fraction of sample pairs from the two zones lying within ε=0.25 of each other (adjacency probability).

Scene-wise HOZ graph: room graphs of the same scene type (kitchen, living room, bedroom, bathroom) are merged pairwise. Each merge solves a weighted bipartite perfect matching with Kuhn–Munkres, using similarity 1/d, where d = Euclidean distance + 1/(δ_k^T δ_j + α) and α=0.1. Matched nodes and edges are then average-pooled. The final HOZ graph is the set of scene-wise graphs, and the scene category is recognized from node features.

Online zone update (per episode, reset each episode): δ(V^t) = λ Z_c f_t^T + (I − λ Z_c Z_c^T) δ(V^{t−1}), with learnable λ. This pulls the current zone's node toward the current observation so the general graph adapts to the unseen room.

Zone localization and planning: the current zone Z_c is the node nearest to f_t under d. The target zone Z_t is the node with the highest occurrence of the target (argmax δ(v_k)^T p). The planner finds the path maximizing the product of edge probabilities from Z_c to Z_t, takes the next node on it as sub-goal Z_sub, and replans whenever the current zone changes.

Graph embeddings: a zone GCN (Kipf-normalized edges, ReLU) gives H_z, and H_z^T Z_sub serves as the sub-goal embedding. An object GCN, following ORG, runs over [bbox, confidence, target one-hot] with a learned adjacency and outputs H_o, which is combined with the detector's per-object visual features as H_o f^v. These are concatenated with the ResNet18 (ImageNet) view feature, the scene embedding and the previous action.

Zone-to-action LSTM policy: trained with A3C (12 workers, 6M episodes, Adam lr 1e-4, reward +5 on success, −0.01 per step). A 'done reminder' weights the Done action by β p^T f^s (the target's detection confidence, β=0.6 initially) to stop in time.
SAE metric: Success weighted by Action Efficiency, i.e. success times the fraction of actions that change location (MoveAhead) among all actions. It penalizes useless rotations that SPL ignores.

setting.backbone: ResNet18 (ImageNet-pretrained, feature extractor) + Faster R-CNN (fine-tuned on AI2-THOR) + zone/object GCNs + LSTM actor-critic trained from scratch with A3C
setting.training_data: AI2-THOR: 80 training rooms (20 per scene type × 4 types), 6M A3C episodes; HOZ graph built from random-exploration observations of the training rooms; Faster R-CNN fine-tuned on 50% of AI2-THOR training data. RoboTHOR: 60 training apartments. Gibson: SemExp setup.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB with detector outputs (AI2-THOR / RoboTHOR); RGB-D + segmentation mask + GPS for the Gibson/SemExp comparison
setting.action_space: discrete {MoveAhead, RotateLeft, RotateRight, LookDown, LookUp, Done}; the agent issues Done itself
setting.privileged: none for the main method (ground-truth detection is used only in one ablation, Table 6; the Gibson variant uses segmentation mask + GPS like SemExp)

RoboTHOR uses a custom train/test split of the public apartments. The Gibson split is not stated.
results: On AI2-THOR, HOZ reaches 70.62 SR / 40.02 SPL / 27.97 SAE, beating the previous best non-adaptive method ORG (66.38/38.42/25.36) and the A3C baseline by +13.27 SR. With self-supervised TPN, HOZ-TPN reaches 73.15 SR vs ORG-TPN's 67.31. On a custom RoboTHOR split, HOZ gets 32.27 SR vs ORG's 29.61 and HOZ-TPN gets 33.28 vs ORG-TPN's 30.01. In Gibson, adding HOZ to SemExp raises SR from 44.01 to 45.19, although Baseline+HOZ alone (43.47) is below SemExp.
limitations: Mainly evaluated on small single-room AI2-THOR scenes; the RoboTHOR test uses a self-made split of public apartments, and the Gibson comparison is small, with the HOZ-only agent underperforming map-based SemExp.

Heavily dependent on object detection quality: ground-truth detection raises SPL by about 18 points in the Table 6 ablation configuration. Zones rely on a fixed cluster count K and on scene-category priors from training rooms.
Online graph adaptation is reset every episode, so no knowledge carries over within an environment. Zone planning uses only coarse adjacency probabilities, not metric geometry.
builds_on: ORG (Object Relation Graph + Tentative Policy Network, Du et al. 2020)
